events.title: The death of St. Swithun
events.shortBlurb: The humble bishop of Winchester was laid, at his own wish, in the open churchyard where the rain might fall upon his grave…
body: St. Swithun was one of the two trusted counsellors of Egbert, King of the West Saxons, who raised him to the see of Winchester about the year 852 and is said to have committed to him the schooling of his son Ethelwulf. The Catholic Encyclopedia, reckoning his death on 2 July 862 — some later authorities give 863 — preserves little of his episcopate, for his fame rests less on deeds than on the humility of his end.

He asked to be buried not within his minster but in the open ground of the churchyard, where the feet of passers-by might tread above him and the rain from the eaves fall upon his grave. There his body rested until 15 July 971, when Bishop Æthelwold translated his relics into the church and raised a shrine in his honor.

From that translation grew his patronage of Winchester Cathedral and the weather-lore that made his name a proverb: St. Swithun's day, if thou dost rain, for forty days it will remain. His shrine, one of the great pilgrim goals of medieval England, was broken up in 1538, when the cult of the saints was swept away; a modern memorial now marks its place.
